The Kiffness V SAMRO

By: Sasha Schwendenwein | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
A musician takes on SAMRO over a lack of music royalty payouts and wins.

Unique Selling Point:
Musician David Scott has a quest: to hold the Royalty music industry to account. He’s quite a character – funny and quirky – our audience would appreciate him - and it’s unique and educational for musicians AND the audience. He has lots of proof and has been quite vocal about it – please see attachments.
This Sunday on Carte Blanche: While the Covid-19 out break has caused many freelancers and creatives to lose work (performances), Musician David Scott aka The Kiffness has found an unusual strategy to keep himself afloat… we follow his investigation into royalty pay-outs in South Africa’s secretive music industry.
MEET Local musician and social media personality David Scott aka The Kiffness …recently known for his humour surrounding the Corona Virus: https://www.facebook.com/thekiffness/videos/236277944217161/, https://www.facebook.com/thekiffness/videos/1291362381252238/, https://www.facebook.com/thekiffness/videos/203506354047381/
But what he isn’t known well for is his massive battle with the music royalty industry. Towards the end of last year Scott went viral for his stringent stance on non-payment of royalties. He came out swinging, calling out 5FM and other radio stations for playing his music but NOT paying him for its use. He basically told them they could no longer play his music as a protest for not being paid (please see vocal tweets and pictures of him protesting) – The industry that are very dependent on radio play/airtime and for positioning on charts like 5fm’s top 40 began to take note – and as his investigations deepened he realized even some the countries biggest artists didn’t understand or know how royalty payments work: mostly because the industry like it that way and they are very secretive. Scott learned about the fact that the SABC hadn’t paid roughly R100 million to SAMPRA https://www.sampra.org.za/ (SA music performance rights association) for radio plays to its roughly 20,000 registered musicians.
And secondly, and more importantly, when he went into his account on SAMRO (SA MUSIC rights organization – which requires proof of radio play to register – once off registration). Scott realized he was not being paying out the correct amounts, or even at all for his performances or needletime (which is another terms for radio plays). Even more disturbing was the fact that someone else –an “David Alexader” (spelt without the N) was being paid his royalties.

Summary:
When he queried this SAMRO said it was “human error”. But when he spoke to other musicians they said ‘doesn’t he know who David Alexander Scott is?’ To his surprise David Alexander (with an N) is strangely a SAMRO board member as well as the founder of Sheer Publishing?!? SAMRO said it was an error, and that David Alexader was an unknown American?!? Scott decided to investigate all his invoices from SAMRO and discovered numerous “human errors” – for example: He had a song that SAMRO said had been paid 14 times, but when he checked on radio monitor (which is very accurate) it was actually played 1300 times. Depending on which station that is, it can be a lot… in that per play is between R60-R400 – and even the amounts were secret and unknown in the industry. SAMRO said it was a “portal error” and that he would be paid for his correct number of radio plays. And when he was paid… it ended up going to “Alexader” again – which they again attributed to “Human error” *we don’t have proof it’s THE David AlexaNder but really? He has all the proof to show that it’s fishy…It’s the same name they constantly keep paying… so it’s worth a question… This is just one example, but he said that it’s a problem rife in the industry. In March this year he wrote open letters to SAMPRA’s CEO Pfanani Lishiva and even woolworths for not paying what was owed to the artists registered with them… (Woolworths haven't broken any rules. They've just opted to use a royalty free service, which they're entitled to do.) These matters were addressed (The SABC are said to be drafting a payment plan with SAMPRA because they received their R2.1 billion government bailout)…and some payments are now forthcoming not just to Scott but other musicians as well… he then created video’s https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=woDGWooQWHY&feature=youtu.be&t=133 and wrote articles

Further information:
https://www.thekiffness.com/2020/5-steps-to-making-sure-you-get-paid-your-samro-royalties around the topic of royalties and it turns out many of his colleagues were having the same issues, or were alerted to the problem, checked their own SAMRO payments and discovered the same issues. Since he has been kicking up such a fuss he realized he was owed hundreds of thousands of rands – and last month was able to claw back a quarter of a million rand. This was shortly after Cape Town announced all musicians concerts and performances would be cancelled due to the Corona Virus. He has continued since them educating others in the industry. And last month his tireless effort paid off – he was paid R250,000 in royalties for just campaigning and learning about the industry I haven't been paid yet. I'm waiting for the money which was paid to the wrong David Scott. Musicians (who were initially too scared to come forward) throughout the industry came out strongly in support of The Kiffness and his efforts to call out different radio stations and the two government organizations responsible for paying royalties – he found out that even artists who had died – like Makeba and Clegg whose estates should benefit were not being paid according to their managers. He wrote this article explaining what his investigation has taught him to educate others in the music industry: https://www.thekiffness.com/2019/how-to-get-paid-the-royalties-owed-to-you-in-south-africa?fbclid=IwAR0o2KxR_KvK1X9sdIENopc7GjFoHuMkxKOIVMJSkNBeOk88mgRC-TeSr4I
•He has tirelessly advocated for SAMRO to be more open in how royalties work – posting what he found out after being in the industry since 2010. Here are the royalty payouts per spin of a song (average) on some of SA's top stations, according to my last SAMRO statement:
METRO FM - R400
947 - R150
Jacaranda 94.2 - R100
Kfm 94.5 - R80
5FM - R60
“Make sure your songs are registered!”
• There are other issues with SAMRO – like the fact that getting registered is problematic in that no one picks up or responds – so you have to go in person, the organization are secretive and don’t give our information or want musicians to be educated, and that very few people even check to see how much they should be paid. Most artists just depend on live performances because it’s trackable and you don’t have to deal with SAMRO – but this has changed due to the coronavirus, so Scott is advocating for education across the music industry at this difficult time. Scott spoke to Karabo Senna & Manqoba Kubheka who are General Managers at SAMRO. When he told them that he heard you can get about R100 / spin they told him that number was too high, but later found out he was right.
Jarrod Assenheim (head of RadioMonitor who monitors radio airplay in South Africa, independent from SAMRO). David has been using radiomonitor and proved there is a huge discrepancy in what SAMRO says about his number of plays. Radiomonitor is working with SAMRO to implement their system. Radio monitor have great stats: chart spins – based on airplay, how many times a song plays, 45% of music played on radio stations is south Africa, which has gone up from 30% when they started 5 years ago... AND that’s increasing during covid 19… as the radio industry are trying to support more during this time… fantastic! Then there is the Rams chart based on listener-ships – 7/8 million listeners and that can tell you how much a song is worth per spin on that station (in peak time for example – higher position on chart etc) Each radio station pays out different loyalty 5c per second to 50/60c per second. Guys who are number one on charts 15-20,000 –R1-2 million for a hit song. Radio air play is still very relevant – compared to Europe and America..They know percentages… and have amazing tech that bots that count the music...
Another case study: Jules Harding from band goodluck who are one of South Africa's top acts... Julz says the industry are uneducated when it comes to royalties= they didn't even know what they should be paid, and what they did get paid was so far off from reality - she currently has employed someone from holland to do an audit of her music to compare it to SAMRO's count. She says musicians are being robbed, there seems to be corruption and the artists (esp small artists) lose. The situation with her of doing a big audit – she said a few years ago samro were caught investing the artists earnings of a billion rand into a scam in dubai which was lost, which was why there was a new SAMRO ceo. It's meant to bea retirement fund. So she was assigned a "music writing expert from SAMRO last year" as Julz is one of the top 100 writers in the country– however, she didn't even know who Julz was, and has only met once in the past year, and the woman knew nothing about songwriting or music. The collecting agency's is an index to tell if an industry is successful or not and SA musicians are so resilient although they are being robbed blind… in another country artists/musicians/songwriters have very good lucrative careers just from publishing but in south africa the only way is to gig big… she says - we have the collection system its just not being paid to artists… This is very similar to what happened to the royalties from sugar man…

Then we have an expert on music industry who is also an artist - and does not want to be named, but will speak with a hidden identity: the info is from analysis of historical performance: He has created figures and graphs. All italics in the spreadsheet are his calcs. The rest are drawn from SAMRO’s annual audited financial statements - all available online with the exception of the 2019 AGM AFS - provided to members via email. It should be noted that the “Royalties written back” line item includes the undocs (undocumented works), public domain and two or three other numbers. In Feb of this year PWC were replaced as SAMRO’s auditors and the numbers you see below for 2018/2019 financial years were restated by the new auditors. I’m not suggesting a causal relationship, just mentioning it as an interesting fact. Here are a few extract from a paper he wrote: “...it is crucial for CMOs to focus on the delivery of their core mandate, in particular effective and efficient income generation and distribution” (2016, p94) and “...in view of the non-profit status of many CMOs there is an obligation to operate in a cost-effective manner
while also generating growing streams of income for members...” Both authors (Hooijer & Baloyi) held executive positions at SAMRO between 1996 and 2011.”
"As SAMRO is competing on a global stage, their efficiency ratios have to be competitive if they are to survive. This can only be addressed through restructuring and finding ways to make the organisation function at a cost-to- revenue ratio of around 15%.

This is one of the most important ratios for members who are interrogating the efficiency of their CMO (Hooijer & Baloyi, 2016)."

"The financial analysis above explains the undocs issue. It is not in SAMRO’s interests to resolve the undocumented works problem. This places the organisation’s interests in conflict with those of the members.

As far as tangible benefit complaints are concerned, besides the undocs issue going some way to explain this, SAMRO does not state its percentage collection rate to members.

The global benchmark for CMO admin costs is around 15%. SAMRO’s admin cost is hovering around 30%, whereas PRS, GEMA, BMI and ASCAP sit between 13% and 15%. All these competitors with the exception of GEMA state the admin fees they charge, whereas SAMRO pays composers a prorated share of remaining revenue after costs (SAMRO, 2019). SAMRO’s costs deducted from revenues are consistently 2-3 times higher (SAMRO 2009-2019) than the globally accepted average of 15% (Hooijer & Baloyi, 2016). This depends whether you define costs as SAMRO's stated admin cost, or the balance remaining after royalties have been paid to members and pension fund amounts allotted"

SAMRO are OPERATING at a loss of between 14-18 million per year… financial ratio’s...SAMRO has an amount sitting on balance sheets which is attributed to undocumented works (UNDOCS) this list is made up of works where they cannot find the owner of the work – the money arrives at SAMRO and either it has been notified incorrectly by author or written down incorrectly on cue sheet – but doesn’t pay it out – list called undocumented works list. Retain money for 3 years and composers are given opportunity to claim, (list is difficult to get) but SAMRO have been putting this money back into their bank account and STRANGELY THEIR financial operating loss EQUALS EXACTLY what they put back into their SAMRO??? It's a massive coincidence… his works were on list this list yet he is a registered artist… he interviewed 15 musicians and everyone had songs on this list... samro issued first version of financials - operating loss equalled royalties written back – then PWC was fired as auditors – (claimed it was a rotation – and new auditors had restated financials and suddenly the undocs no longer equalled operating loss)
**Financial analyst – current ratio versus operating cash flow ratio.. BANKRUPT…

Press Release:


A Modern Tale of David vs. Goliath
Imagine there was over R250,000 due to you in royalties and you didn’t know. That was the case for popular musician David Scott – better known as The Kiffness – after he discovered just how much he was owed in music royalties. Now he’s a man on a mission, taking on an industry that’s become notorious for underpaying artists and performers and he’s inspiring other musicians to fight back.
Producer: Sasha Schwendenwein | Presenter: Derek Watts


Script:


Making it in the music industry is hard, but South Africa’s roughly 20,000 registered musicians are finding it even harder during the lockdown...
David Scott: A lot of musicians their main source of income which is live shows has dried up.
Which has led some musicians to look elsewhere...
IMAGINE A QUARTER OF A MILLION RANDS IN ROYALTIES JUST COLLECTING IN A BANK ACCOUNT…AND YOU DIDN’T KNOW. THAT’S WHAT SPURRED ONE MUSIC ACT – THE KIFFNESS – TO INVESTIGATE THE SECRETIVE MUSIC BUSINESS.
[Trumpet] Hi im David Scott, the kiffness I’m a music producer from cape town...
Scott: I play the trumpet. My band mate plays saxophone and we kind of overlaid that of a sort of electronic beats, but now that it's lockdown the Kiffness is probably more well known for making parodies...
SHOW TWO PARADIES…
WHEN YOU HEAR A SONG ON THE RADIO OR AT AN EVENT …YOU MIGHT NOT BE AWARE THAT THE AUTHORS OF THAT MUSIC – PUBLISHER, RECORD COMPANIES, COMPOSERS, SONGWRITERS, VOCALISTS AND ARTISTS -ALL EARN A FEE FOR THE USE OF THEIR PATENT (OR WORK) …EVERY TIME IT’S PLAYED – THIS IS CALLED A ROYALTY FEE.
Collective management organisations or CMO’s recover royalties on behalf of musicians for an admin fee. Scott zeroed in on The Southern African Music Rights Organisation or SAMRO and SAMPRA - the South African Music Performance Rights Association. SAMPRA’s CEO Pfanani Lishivha explains the complexity of royalty’s.
Lishivha: Music users that are licensed by SAMRO are the same music users that we license, the SAMRO fee goes to the author the composer and the publisher of the song while the SAMPRA fee goes to the record company that owns the track as well as he performers that performed when that particular song was recorded.
Scott: If you've had your stuff play on your radio or even in restaurants or retail stores make sure that you're registered. You try to sign up and then you never hear back from them, so have to kind of put on your Derek watts pants on.
Scott catalogued his journey on social media to bring awareness to the issues surrounding music royalties.
Scott: Sort of halfway through last year I was made aware of the fact that I had unclaimed royalties at Sampra.
In order to register you need to submit membership forms, but Scott became frustrated when his were lost twice. So he went in person to SAMPRA.
Scott: And then while I was trying to explain myself to this lady at Sampra she realized who I was And then she sang me the song I said Yes that's me. and she literally made me a member within three minutes. I've been paid in the region of R150 to R200,000
Lishivha has made many changes this year, including reducing SAMPRAs admin fee from 20 to 17%.
Lishivha: we are the only CMO in South Africa right now that allows for online applications. We are also the only CMO, in the whole world that has got a mobile app.
Scott’s investigation brought the battle between SAMPRA and the SABC to light.
Scott: The SABC owes SAMPRA in the region of 100 million rand. that's when I decided I'm just not going to let the SABC play my music until they've paid Sampra. Some would say it's career suicide but, started a petition called Hashtag no pay no play, That got 8000 signatures and it got the attention of the Honourable Swarts in Parliament.
Swart: “One of the areas of concern, is the payment of royalties to musicians and others who have rendered a service to the SABC…”
THE SABC DECLINED AN ON-CAMERA INTERVIEW OPTING INSTEAD TO REPLY IN WRITING THEY SAY THEY PAID AN AMOUNT OF 17 MILLION RANDS FOR OUTSTANDING ROYALTIES
which were paid to another royalty collection company. The SABC remains committed to paying royalties, but there is an ongoing dispute with SAMPRA relating to the formula they used to calculate the royalties, and are unable to pay until the dispute is resolved.
Lishivha: We haven't received a cent from the SABC in the last three years.
SAMPRA are NOW considering pulling their song playlist - which represents 90 percent of all our local artists. Scott THEN turned his attention to SAMRO
Scott: Some of my biggest songs which were on the radio I haven't been paid for. Find A Way and You Say You Love Me just didn’t show up on this list. There was a song – say you love me – which isn’t my song. [Trumpet upsound] This is one of the songs I wasn’t paid for and I finally got paid in the region of R30,000 for this song.
Scott found song count inconsistencies and turned to the independent monitoring service for help, run by Jarrod Aston-Assenheim.
Jarrod: Radio monitor is a system that provides accurate data in order for artists to understand exactly how many times they’ve been played, on which radio stations, to ensure that they get paid royalties that they’re due. It's very similar to the way the AP Shazam works. We basically listen to what's being played and we match it to what we have in our system to what's being played on the radio system.
Scott: so this is the latest song that did well on the radio last year, it played about 1300 times, samro reported SAMRO reported that it has only been played 14 times. I found out now im owed about 30,000 it would have just disappeared. during this whole investigation I found out that they had somehow incorrectly paid the wrong David Scott, someone called David Alexader Scott..
UPSOUND: This is a list of all the songs with Scott Alexader and if I add that all up that’s R41,000 rand.
SAMRO claims this was human error and reversed it, BUT it’s since happened 3 more times. Nicholas Mawena - SAMROs new chair - appointed last year welcomes artists to settle disputes.
Mawena: If there was an error it has been corrected and I believe in particular the Kiffnis, we've resolved that particular matter with him.
But this. Mr. Alexander was paid three more times it seems?
Mawena: That's very unfortunate. And if this matter's reoccurring and find out why
Mawena says the song count discrepancies have been fixed.
Derek: But that's a massive error, it's not a slight miscount must be a massive error.
Mawena: Once it was identified the most important thing. It's been corrected
Derek: It shouldn't be the members responsibility. You should be providing a service of collecting royalties?
Mawena: I think the matter could easily be resolved. we then do an investigation and find out who really made that error.
Many artists contacted Scott with similar issues like SAMA winner, Goodluck, whose lead vocalist is Julz Harding. And singer Majozi - who has topped South Africa’s chart shows with hit songs like Darling...
Julz: We've had to enlist the services of a company in the Netherlands who are charging us by the hour to basically cross-reference our statements without actual factual monitored radio reports from radio monitor.
Majozi: The kiffness brought awareness to me… he told me exactly what I must do and it paid off. I’ve received around R100,000…
And that was for the 6 years worth of royalties.
and that’s money that has been really good for my career and helped me out a lot, money that I really needed.
Another easy way for artists to claim royalties is to regularly check the UNDOCS list.
UNDOCUMENTED WORKS OR UNCLAIMED ROYALTIES WHERE AN ARTIST HIS NAME BUT CANNOT BE TRACED BY THE COLLECTION AGENCY SO THE ONUS TO CHECK WHETHER ON THE LIST RESTS WITH THE ARTIST
Derek: Some well-known artists on the list. Johnny Clegg, PJ powers, Kwesta?
Mawena: If the individuals that you've mentioned come to Samro and really lodge a claim we normally do make the payment.
SAMRO may partner with Radio Monitor to correct these issues.
INTRO TO FINANCIALS: A SOURCE ENTRUSTED CARTE BLANCHE WITH DOCUMENTS THAT PAINT A DISTURBING PICTURE OF SAMROS FINANCIALS. THE MORE DISTURBING QUESTION IS HOW THE NPO GOT INTO SUCH DEEP FINANCIAL TROUBLE.
Mawena: We arrived and we found a couple of challenges within Samro, I was brought in as the independent chair to make sure that we preside over this.
Derek: Nicholas last year's financials showed a 36 percent admin fee. Now that's huge?
Mawena: we wanted to at least be in the region of about 25 percent it's part of our as this new board in terms of a strategy for us is really we are looking at efficiency.√
Julz: I don't feel like it's transparent enough At the end of the day, that's coming straight out of the pocket of musicians who are really struggle.
SAMRO is becoming more transparent by publishing how much each radio station pays per play of a song.
Mawena: a member now can work out for themselves and really double check us.
To help local artists earn even more royalties, radio stations are upping their airtime by 5%.
Majozi: if the money could just get into the artists hands it would really help them during this lockdown just to pay for groceries and things that they really need right now.
Scott says he’ll continue to fight the lockdown blues … (put a parody) https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=DMDH4ll_vq4

PROMO 1: David Scott’s lockdown parodies have made these long days easier…(soundup) but what you might not know is he’s a man on mission - taking on the music royalty industry.
PROMO 2: You may know The Kiffness for his lockdown parodies, but the music industry knows him for fighting to make royalty agencies more transparent.
PROMO 3: Imagine over R250,000 due to you in royalty's and you didn’t know. That’s what happened to one musician who investigates the business of music royalties.

Now he’s a man on a mission, taking on an industry that’s become notorious for underpaying artists and performers and he’s inspiring other musicians to fight back. David Scott: A lot of musicians their main source of income which is live shows has dried up. Which has led some musicians to look elsewhere... Collective management organisations or CMO’s recover royalties on behalf of musicians for an admin fee. Scott: If you've had your stuff play on your radio or even in restaurants or retail stores make sure that you're registered. metadata.Unique Selling Point: Musician David Scott has a quest: to hold the Royalty music industry to account. He’s quite a character – funny and quirky – our audience would appreciate him - and it’s unique and educational for musicians AND the audience. He has lots of proof and has been quite vocal about it – please see attachments. This Sunday on Carte Blanche: While the Covid-19 out break has caused many freelancers and creatives to lose work (performances), Musician David Scott aka The Kiffness has found an unusual strategy to keep himself afloat… we follow his investigation into royalty pay-outs in South Africa’s secretive music industry. MEET Local musician and social media personality David Scott aka The Kiffness …recently known for his humour surrounding the Corona Virus: https://www.facebook.com/thekiffness/videos/236277944217161/, https://www.facebook.com/thekiffness/videos/1291362381252238/, https://www.facebook.com/thekiffness/videos/203506354047381/ But what he isn’t known well for is his massive battle with the music royalty industry. Towards the end of last year Scott went viral for his stringent stance on non-payment of royalties. He came out swinging, calling out 5FM and other radio stations for playing his music but NOT paying him for its use. He basically told them they could no longer play his music as a protest for not being paid (please see vocal tweets and pictures of him protesting) – The industry that are very dependent on radio play/airtime and for positioning on charts like 5fm’s top 40 began to take note – and as his investigations deepened he realized even some the countries biggest artists didn’t understand or know how royalty payments work: mostly because the industry like it that way and they are very secretive. Scott learned about the fact that the SABC hadn’t paid roughly R100 million to SAMPRA https://www.sampra.org.za/ (SA music performance rights association) for radio plays to its roughly 20,000 registered musicians. And secondly, and more importantly, when he went into his account on SAMRO (SA MUSIC rights organization – which requires proof of radio play to register – once off registration). Scott realized he was not being paying out the correct amounts, or even at all for his performances or needletime (which is another terms for radio plays). Even more disturbing was the fact that someone else –an “David Alexader” (spelt without the N) was being paid his royalties.
metadata.Summary: When he queried this SAMRO said it was “human error”. But when he spoke to other musicians they said ‘doesn’t he know who David Alexander Scott is?’ To his surprise David Alexander (with an N) is strangely a SAMRO board member as well as the founder of Sheer Publishing?!? SAMRO said it was an error, and that David Alexader was an unknown American?!? Scott decided to investigate all his invoices from SAMRO and discovered numerous “human errors” – for example: He had a song that SAMRO said had been paid 14 times, but when he checked on radio monitor (which is very accurate) it was actually played 1300 times. Depending on which station that is, it can be a lot… in that per play is between R60-R400 – and even the amounts were secret and unknown in the industry. SAMRO said it was a “portal error” and that he would be paid for his correct number of radio plays. And when he was paid… it ended up going to “Alexader” again – which they again attributed to “Human error” *we don’t have proof it’s THE David AlexaNder but really? He has all the proof to show that it’s fishy…It’s the same name they constantly keep paying… so it’s worth a question… This is just one example, but he said that it’s a problem rife in the industry. In March this year he wrote open letters to SAMPRA’s CEO Pfanani Lishiva and even woolworths for not paying what was owed to the artists registered with them… (Woolworths haven't broken any rules. They've just opted to use a royalty free service, which they're entitled to do.) These matters were addressed (The SABC are said to be drafting a payment plan with SAMPRA because they received their R2.1 billion government bailout)…and some payments are now forthcoming not just to Scott but other musicians as well… he then created video’s https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=woDGWooQWHY&feature=youtu.be&t=133 and wrote articles
